name: Satan
interpretive_note: Interpreters differ on whether every occurrence of "satan"/"the satan" throughout the Old and New Testaments describes one single fallen angel with a continuous identity and history, or whether some Old Testament instances (particularly the accusing figure in the heavenly court of Job 1-2) function more as a title or role within the divine council. The New Testament clearly presents a single personal adversary (the devil, the ancient serpent, the dragon); this article follows Scripture's own consistent naming across both testaments while noting the Old Testament usage is debated among scholars.
source_summary: The accuser and adversary who incited David to take a sinful census, tested Job's faithfulness, tempted Jesus in the wilderness, and opposes God's people throughout Scripture until his final judgment in Revelation.
family_friendly_summary: Satan (a name that means "accuser" or "adversary") is the Bible's name for the being who opposes God and tries to lead people away from Him. We first meet him testing Job's faith by bringing him terrible troubles, always within limits God set. He also tried to tempt Jesus to sin when Jesus was alone in the wilderness for forty days -- but Jesus resisted every temptation by trusting God's word. Throughout the Bible, Satan is described as a liar, an accuser, and an enemy of God's people, but he is never shown to be equal to God in power. The Bible's story ends with Satan's complete and final defeat, judged forever, while God's people live safely with Him.
adult_story: Satan (Hebrew for "adversary") first appears by that name accusing Job before God's heavenly court, testing whether Job's faithfulness would survive the loss of everything he had -- though Job never once curses God (Job 1-2). In 1 Chronicles 21:1, Satan incites David to take a sinful census of Israel, bringing God's judgment on the nation; the parallel account in 2 Samuel 24:1 attributes the same event to the LORD's anger, an unresolved tension Scripture leaves standing rather than explaining away. In Zechariah's vision, "the satan" stands to accuse the high priest Joshua before the LORD's angel, only to be rebuked (Zechariah 3:1-2). The New Testament names him plainly as tempter: after Jesus's baptism, Satan tested Him three times in the wilderness with appeals to appetite, presumption, and power, and each time Jesus answered from Scripture and refused (Matthew 4:1-11). Jesus calls him "a liar and the father of lies" and "a murderer from the beginning" (John 8:44), and Paul warns that he disguises himself "as an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14). Satan entered Judas before the betrayal (Luke 22:3) and demanded to sift Peter "like wheat" (Luke 22:31). Revelation portrays him as the great dragon, deceiver of the nations, whose defeat is already secured by Christ and who will finally be "thrown into the lake of fire" forever (Revelation 20:10) -- Scripture's real but always subordinate, already-defeated enemy.
